children: Namita Patwari says lasting change needs employee involvement, visible leadership commitment and open feedback, and that the real test of a cultural shift is what people do when no one is reminding them of the new behaviours

At 115 years old, Alembic Pharmaceuticals is evolving without letting go of what defines it. Namita Patwari, CHRO and Chief Customer Experience Officer, says HR’s job is to protect trust, integrity, commitment and purpose while building the digital fluency, analytical thinking and adaptability pharma will need. She explains how AI-enabled learning through RepReadyAI is strengthening field execution, why wellbeing must be built into how work is organised and not run as a stand-alone programme, and why a culture has truly shifted only when people act on new behaviours without being reminded. She also outlines what HR should do early to make mergers and partnerships work, beginning with listening.
A 115-year-old company keeps evolving without losing its identity. Which elements of a long-standing culture should HR deliberately protect as the business changes?

The strength of a legacy organisation lies in evolving while staying true to its values. At Alembic, over a century of growth has been guided by trust, integrity, commitment, and purpose. HR plays a key role in preserving this legacy while adapting to changing employee expectations and business needs. Culture is reflected in everyday actions, leadership decisions, and how employees feel respected, valued, and included. A strong legacy fosters belonging and pride while creating opportunities for growth, enabling employees to contribute meaningfully to the organisation’s future.
Which capabilities will pharma need most over the next five years, and how should HR build them across R&D, manufacturing, and commercial teams?

I believe the pharmaceutical industry will increasingly require digital fluency, analytical thinking, technical expertise, and adaptability. Equally important is the ability to learn continuously and apply knowledge effectively in everyday work. At Alembic, our RepReadyAI initiative reflects how technology can make learning more interactive, practical, and engaging.

For me, the real value of learning lies not in completing a programme, but in how confidently employees apply their knowledge, improve their performance, and grow in their roles. Learning outcomes should be measurable through stronger on-the-job application, improved productivity, enhanced quality of execution, and increased readiness for larger responsibilities.

HR must create opportunities for continuous learning through relevant development programmes, practical exposure, and regular feedback. We must also help employees prepare for evolving responsibilities and future career opportunities. Equally important is tracking the effectiveness of learning through indicators such as skill proficiency, performance improvements, internal mobility, succession readiness, and the successful application of new capabilities in the workplace. When people are equipped to grow alongside the business and learning outcomes are translated into tangible results, capability building becomes an investment in both individual development and organisational resilience.
As AI takes over more routine HR work, how will the role of the CHRO change in the next few years?

I see AI as an opportunity to make HR more proactive, efficient, and data-driven by simplifying routine processes and enabling greater focus on leadership development, workforce planning, capability building, and employee experience. In pharma, AI can help identify skill gaps across functions, anticipate future capability needs, personalise learning, and strengthen talent pipelines. At Alembic, RepReadyAI demonstrates how AI-enabled, practice-based learning can strengthen scientific knowledge, customer engagement, and field execution among sales representatives.

However, the human dimension of HR will remain critical. While AI can provide insights, understanding employee aspirations, building trust, coaching leaders, and making sensitive people decisions require empathy and judgement. CHROs must ensure technology complements human capabilities while helping employees develop digital fluency and adaptability.

Ultimately, AI’s value must be measured through tangible outcomes, including faster onboarding and hiring, improved learning effectiveness and field productivity, stronger GMP and compliance training adherence, better succession readiness, and enhanced employee engagement. Used thoughtfully, AI can enable better decisions and build a more agile, responsive, and future-ready organisation.
How can wellbeing become part of the way work is organised, rather than a stand-alone programme?

I believe wellbeing is shaped by everyday work experiences-how we respect people’s time, understand their needs, and support them through different stages of life. At Alembic, the eight-hour workday and period-related work-from-home flexibility reflect this focus. I believe such measures recognise employees’ diverse needs and responsibilities while enabling them to contribute effectively.

For me, a supportive culture also means creating an environment where employees can raise concerns comfortably and managers lead with empathy. For example, a manager adjusting a deadline when an employee faces a personal challenge demonstrates how small, thoughtful actions can make wellbeing part of everyday work. Policies provide the framework, but their impact lies in how they are practised. I believe wellbeing must be reflected in daily decisions, team interactions, and opportunities for growth and not treated as a stand-alone HR initiative.
With your grounding in organisation development, what makes a change initiative last, and what tells you a culture has genuinely shifted?

One of the most important lessons I have learnt is that change cannot be sustained through communication alone. People embrace change when they understand its purpose, see its relevance to their work, and witness leaders consistently demonstrating the expected behaviours. In my experience, lasting change requires employee involvement, visible leadership commitment, and opportunities to share feedback and concerns. When employees feel heard and included, they take ownership rather than view change as something imposed on them.

For me, a real cultural shift is reflected in everyday actions like how teams collaborate, take accountability, make decisions, and express different viewpoints. While engagement scores and employee feedback are useful indicators, I believe the true measure of success lies in what people do when no one is reminding them what the new behaviours should be. Change becomes sustainable when these behaviours become part of the organisation's way of working and are reflected naturally in how people think, interact and contribute every day. That, to me, is when culture has genuinely evolved.
As companies grow through partnerships and acquisitions, what should HR put in place early so that different cultures come together well?

I believe successful cultural integration begins with listening. Every organisation has its own strengths, values and working styles, and HR should understand these before deciding how to bring people together. A culture and working-style assessment of both organisations, done early, gives integration decisions a factual base. Early on, HR must give clarity on roles, reporting lines, communication channels and growth opportunities, and commit to timelines for each. Uncertainty is where people disengage or leave, so concerns should be addressed openly, with critical talent engaged first and regular forums such as town halls and Q&As where employees can ask questions and get honest answers.

I would place strong emphasis on leadership alignment. Leaders from both sides should present a consistent message and model the behaviours expected. A joint integration team, along with cross-team projects built around shared goals, helps relationships form through real work. Integration should not mean overlooking the strengths each group brings; the aim is to keep what works from both and build a common purpose people can connect with. Ultimately, integration succeeds when employees see a place for themselves in the organisation’s future and understand how they can contribute to it. That sense of belonging is what holds a combined organisation together.
Savi Khanna
